4. Continuity

Continuity via ε-δ, uniform continuity, and the great theorems: the intermediate and extreme value theorems.

  • The ε–δ Definition — The rigorous meaning of lim⁡x→af(x)=L\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = Llimx→a​f(x)=L: no matter how narrow the ε\varepsilonε-band, there is a δ\deltaδ-band around aaa where fff stays inside it. Check δ=ε/2\delta = \varepsilon/2δ=ε/2 for f(x)=2xf(x) = 2xf(x)=2x, a=1a = 1a=1, L=2L = 2L=2.
  • The Definition of Continuity — fff is continuous at aaa when lim⁡x→af(x)=f(a)\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)limx→a​f(x)=f(a) — the limit and the value must agree. Move the point aaa; in broken mode the value at one point is lifted and the definition breaks.
  • Thomae's Function — The popcorn function f(p/q)=1/qf(p/q) = 1/qf(p/q)=1/q (reduced), f(x)=0f(x) = 0f(x)=0 (irrational): continuous at every irrational, discontinuous at every rational. Given ε\varepsilonε, only finitely many dots reach height ε\varepsilonε — so near an irrational a δ\deltaδ can always be found.
  • Three Faces of Continuity — Continuity has three faces: the ε\varepsilonε-δ\deltaδ argument, the sequential test, and preimages of open sets. Placing f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 next to a jump function shows the three faces saying the same thing.
  • Discontinuities of Monotone Functions — A monotone function has left and right limits everywhere, so every discontinuity is a jump. Only finitely many jumps can exceed 1/n1/n1/n, so the discontinuities are at most countable — no matter how many there are.
  • Uniform Continuity — Uniform continuity demands one δ\deltaδ that works at every point xxx — δ\deltaδ may depend on ε\varepsilonε alone, never on xxx. Watch the required δ\deltaδ shrink as xxx grows for f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2, so no single δ\deltaδ covers all of R\mathbb{R}R.
  • You Can't Climb Without Crossing Every Height — A continuous function on [a,b][a,b][a,b] must step on every value between f(a)f(a)f(a) and f(b)f(b)f(b). Move the target level ccc and find the crossing ξ\xiξ.
  • The Extreme Value Theorem — A continuous function on a closed interval always attains its max and min. Verify it for f(x)=x3−3xf(x) = x^3 - 3xf(x)=x3−3x on [−2,2][-2,2][−2,2], and see from the open-interval and discontinuous counterexamples that both hypotheses are necessary.
  • When the Limit Breaks — fn(x)=xnf_n(x)=x^nfn​(x)=xn converges at every point of [0,1][0,1][0,1], yet sup⁡∣fn−f∣=1↛0\sup|f_n-f|=1\not\to 0sup∣fn​−f∣=1→0: not uniformly. Watch the limit break at x=1x=1x=1.
